title: Network formation and dynamics among multi-LLMs

key_points.claim: Framework studies network formation by multiple LLM agents and benchmarks against humans; LLMs reproduce micro-level principles (preferential attachment, triadic closure, homophily) and macro-level properties (community structure, small-world).
key_points.evidence_quote: LLMs reproduce core microlevel principles (preferential attachment, triadic closure, and homophily), and macrolevel properties (community structure, small-world effects).

key_points.claim: LLM link preferences are context-dependent: homophily in friendship networks, heterophily in organizational settings.
key_points.evidence_quote: LLMs favor homophily in friendship networks but heterophily in organizational settings, mirroring patterns of social mobility.

key_points.claim: A controlled survey shows strong alignment between LLM and human link-formation decisions; suggested use for social simulation and synthetic data, with bias/fairness risks.
key_points.evidence_quote: A controlled survey shows strong alignment between LLM and human link-formation decisions.

key_points.claim: Method: independent LLM agents in separate conversational threads, sequentially adding nodes (n=200) with full network info in the prompt; varied models, temperature, and prompting; extended to real friendship, telecom, and company collaboration networks.
key_points.evidence_quote: By simulating multiple LLM agents acting independently within separate conversational threads, we examined their behaviors in decision-making scenarios involving network connections.

key_points.claim: Preferential attachment tested against a random-connection null model, with power-law exponents estimated across model, temperature, and environment.
key_points.evidence_quote: we compare these probabilities to a null model assuming random connections

key_points.claim: Context: prior work shows LLM collectives can exhibit linguistic conventions and the friendship paradox; ABM with LLMs is an emerging approach.
key_points.evidence_quote: collectives of LLMs can exhibit linguistic conventions ([26], [27]) and even the friendship paradox ([28])

reliability_notes: Full text fetched from peer-reviewed journal (PNAS Nexus, 2025). I read the abstract, introduction and start of the results. I did not read the later results, the discussion or the methods in detail. Findings rely mainly on GPT-family models, and the paper does not claim that its results generalize to every LLM.
